authority.text: The selected source illuminates a commemorating family and a trading city rather than defining an imperial dynasty.

evidence.text: A funerary relief preserves named kin and a chosen visual identity; it is not a census of the city.

coordination.text: Kinship display, civic fiscal decisions and caravan commemoration organized different relationships. The tariff concerns recurring local transactions; distant commercial roles require their own records.

name: Palmyra

interval.label: 2nd–3rd centuries CE

question: Can a family portrait illuminate a trading city?
summary: A family memorial, a public tariff and caravan inscriptions make different people visible in Palmyra. Stone carving and kinship display belonged to a city whose officials regulated local exchange while merchants worked through wider networks. Reading these records together connects family choices, civic institutions and ordinary transactions. Their differences matter: a named portrait does not identify a caravan leader, and a tax rule does not describe every journey.

sections.title: Names made a family memorable
sections.text: The selected relief identifies Zabdibol, his son Mokimu and daughters Tadmur and Alayyat. Its Aramaic inscription also sets out the father’s ancestry. A reclining figure, smaller companions, clothing and objects turn kinship into a durable image within a tomb. The Met interprets the stone as probably closing a family burial niche. Commissioning and carving such a memorial required resources and skilled work. Its carefully arranged banquet presents a chosen remembrance, rather than recording an ordinary meal or the household’s entire membership.

citations.locator: Inscription, banquet description and burial marker

sections.title: The city regulated recurring transactions
sections.text: In 137 CE the council published revised tax rules alongside older provisions to address disputes about charges. Greek and Palmyrene Aramaic versions made civic decisions visible in different forms of writing. The tariff includes local goods and services, not merely distant luxuries. Matthews discusses mobile clothing sellers, workshops and produce moving between villages and the city. Such evidence brings routine exchange into a history otherwise dominated by monumental tombs and famous caravans. The regulation shows what officials sought to organize; it does not establish universal compliance.

sections.title: Long-distance exchange needed its own evidence
sections.text: Honorific inscriptions commemorating caravan leaders and supporters provide a separate record of commercial organization. The Getty discussion connects trading communities beyond the city with river and overland movement. A network depended on storage, distribution and intermediaries, not just a line between famous capitals. The named family in this relief is not thereby proved to have financed those journeys. Compare a family’s claim to remembered identity with a public record praising someone’s commercial contribution: each selects a different accomplishment and audience.

citations.locator: Trade: caravan inscriptions and trading communities

sections.title: One city held more than one kind of writing
sections.text: Public bilingual texts and private funerary inscriptions had different purposes. An inscription can preserve a name, obligation or civic decision without measuring how many residents could read. Children’s images sometimes support questions about education, but another relief’s writing tablet cannot be transferred to this family. The two sieges of 272 and 273 damaged the city and changed its position. They did not erase all later habitation. This longer sequence lets the second–third-century object remain a bounded family inquiry within a changing city.

deeperReading.title: Compare inscriptions without merging their people
deeperReading.text: Sokołowski studies a different relief, Berlin 27/65, depicting a boy and girl with inscriptions. His account proposes that a handled tablet could signal education and discusses a word that may mean tutor, guardian or household steward. These are interpretations of that object, not a biography supplied for Zabdibol’s children. The selected Met stone has its own names and composition. Comparing the two shows how image, text and an interpreter’s contextual knowledge work together; it cannot establish every child’s literacy, actual curriculum or age. The source’s hypotheses about languages learned and private teaching remain hypotheses.

deeperReading.title: Do not reduce an oasis city to a transit stop
deeperReading.text: Local production, grazing, markets and village supplies belong alongside long-distance commerce. Matthews’s excerpt warns against treating the tariff as if it concerned only caravans. Meanwhile, honorific records favor people worth commemorating publicly. The two source groups should therefore be compared rather than ranked as interchangeable measures of prosperity. A household able to purchase carved stone is also not a representative sample of all households. Further work should examine archaeological neighborhoods, workshops, gendered labor and enslaved people, and distinguish fiscal categories from what people actually experienced. None of the sources consulted here yields a defensible city-wide income or literacy rate.

items.label: The selected memorial names kin
items.text: The Met identifies Zabdibol, his son Mokimu, daughters Tadmur and Alayyat, and a line of paternal ancestors.
items.interpretation: The supplied reading supports named relationships. It does not identify this family’s occupation or a route taken by its members.

items.label: A civic decree addresses charges
items.text: The 137 tariff sets revised and earlier fiscal provisions in a public civic context.
items.interpretation: A municipal regulation is different evidence from the honorific inscriptions associated with caravans. The Greek text also has gaps and editorial supplements.

items.label: A different child holds a tablet
items.text: The Hamburg essay discusses two children on Berlin 27/65 and offers a qualified interpretation of a writing tablet.
items.interpretation: Those children and their proposed education do not become the biography of the Met relief’s figures. An image of a tablet is not a city-wide literacy survey.

placeStudy.title: Palmyra: a city within an exchange network
placeStudy.description: Approximate city locators follow the consulted account’s trading-post sequence. The dashed connection is schematic: it does not reproduce an excavated road, every intermediary or the journey of Zabdibol’s family. Civic transactions and local supply also mattered within the city.

points.label: Antioch — Mediterranean-facing exchange
points.text: The Met describes routes from Antioch across the Syrian Desert through Palmyra to Ctesiphon. The point marks Antioch’s city area. The route account gives no findspot for a particular cargo.

points.label: Palmyra — families and civic exchange
points.text: The memorial, local tax regulation and caravan records belong to different activities. None establishes the selected family’s occupation or a complete itinerary.

points.label: Ctesiphon — a Mesopotamian trading setting
points.text: The Met names Ctesiphon in the wider sequence of distribution. A line between these locators is not evidence that one person carried a shipment through every place.
